We first simplify the given equations, and get

I. $\operatorname{csc} x=10$

II. $\operatorname{csc} x=\frac{1}{3}$

III. $\operatorname{csc} x=4$

Now, recall that the range of $\operatorname{csc} x$ for $0\le x<2\pi$ is given by

$$
\operatorname{csc} x\in (-\mathrm{∞},-1]\cup [1,\mathrm{∞}).
$$

So, the equation $\operatorname{csc} x=k$ has no solutions for $k\in (-1,1).$ 

Therefore, of the given equations, only equation II has no solutions.

Let $y={e}^{\lambda x}.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+8{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8=0.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +2)(\lambda +4)=0,
$$

and so $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =-4.$ 

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{-4x}.
$$

The parametric equations of the line take the general form

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &={x}_{0}+{v}_{x}t \\ y &={y}_{0}+{v}_{y}t \\ z &={z}_{0}+{v}_{z}t,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}{v}_{x} \\ {v}_{y} \\ {v}_{z}\end{bmatrix}$ is the direction vector of the line and $\mathbf{p}=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{0} \\ {y}_{0} \\ {z}_{0}\end{bmatrix}$ is the position vector of a point that lies in the line.

From the parametric equations of the line, we obtain that its vector equation is 

$$
\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the image of the line $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{p}+t\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$, we need to compute the images of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}) & =T\,\mathbf{p} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) & =T\,\mathbf{v} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the image is $\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\mathrm{∞},\mathrm{∞}).
$$

From the Cartesian equation of our line, we obtain that its vector equation is 

$$
\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the image of the line $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{p}+t\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$, we need to compute the images of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}) & =T\,\mathbf{p} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) & =T\,\mathbf{v} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the image is $\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.$

differences.source:
First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global minimum of a function is the smallest value that the function attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global minimum.

- A global minimum point of a function is a point $(x,y)$ where a function reaches a global minimum. There can be zero, one, or many global minimum points.

For our function, the minimum value reached by the function is $f(x)=-7.$ Therefore, the global minimum is $-7.$ The function reaches this value at $x=-12.$

Which of the following functions are bijections?

I. $f:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=|x|$

II. $g:\mathbb{Q}\to \mathbb{Q}$ defined by $g(x)=4(x-2)$

III. $h:\mathbb{Q}\to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $h(x)=\operatorname{sin} x$
differences.stored:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y=0.
$$

differences.source:
Recall that a function $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

- I is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. For example, there is no value $x\in \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x)=-1.$

- II is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $\mathrm{∀}\,y\in \mathbb{Q},$ we can choose an $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $g(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =y \\ 4(x-2) & =y \\ x & =\frac{y}{4}+2\in \mathbb{Q}\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that, 

$$
g(x)=g\left(\frac{y}{4}+2\right)=4\left(\left[\frac{y}{4}+2\right]-2\right)=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ 4({x}_{1}-2) & =4({x}_{2}-2) \\ {x}_{1}-2 & ={x}_{2}-2 \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because $g$ is both surjective and injective, $g$ is bijective.

- III is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $\operatorname{sin} x$ is $[-1,1].$ This means that 

$$
-1\le \operatorname{sin} x\le 1.
$$

So,  for example, there is no value $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $h(x)=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}-6{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -6) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -6.
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +3)(\lambda -2)=0,
$$

and so $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =2.$ 

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation is

$$
y=A{e}^{-3x}+B{e}^{2x}.
$$

First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global minimum of a function is the smallest value that the function attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global minimum.

- A global minimum point of a function is a point $(x,y)$ where a function reaches a global minimum. There can be zero, one, or many global minimum points.

For our function, the minimum value reached by the function is $f(x)=-2.$ Therefore, the global minimum is $-2.$ The function reaches this value at $x=0.$

Recall that a function $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

- I is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. For example, there is no value $x\in \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x)=-1.$

- II is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $\mathrm{∀}\,y\in \mathbb{Q},$ we can choose an $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $g(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =y \\ 4(x-2) & =y \\ x & =\frac{y}{4}+2\in \mathbb{Q}\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that, 

$$
g(x)=g\left(\frac{y}{4}+2\right)=4\left(\left[\frac{y}{4}+2\right]-2\right)=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ 4({x}_{1}-2) & =4({x}_{2}-2) \\ {x}_{1}-2 & ={x}_{2}-2 \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Because $g$ is both surjective and injective, $g$ is bijective.

- III is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $\operatorname{sin} x$ is $[-1,1].$ This means that 

$$
-1\le \operatorname{sin} x\le 1.
$$

So,  for example, there is no value $x\in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $h(x)=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,l:\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

differences.source:
To find the image of the line $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{p}+t\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$, we need to compute the images of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}) & =T\,\mathbf{p} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) & =T\,\mathbf{v} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the image is $\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

$$

differences.source:
Let's examine each statement.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ decreases on the left-hand side of the graph, the function continues to increase without bound (as indicated by the arrow). So, the function does not reach a global maximum value.

- Statement II is false. As $x$ increases on the right-hand side of the graph, the function continues to decrease without bound (as indicated by the arrow). So, the function does not reach a global minimum value.

- Statement III is true. The function does not have a global maximum and does not have a global minimum. Therefore, the function does not have any global extrema.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."
